_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 5 specification (about 600 words, six questions in text order: detail/opinion, inference, reference, purpose, meaning of a phrase, and a final question that links the ending back to the opening). Each card is a chunk of the article with the question it answers; `highlight` is the sentence that proves the answer, `why` explains the distractors. Used by the Part 5 practice page.
title: The bike is just the excuse
subtitle: Retired pharmacist Hanna Brook repairs unwanted bicycles and gives them to refugee families. Priya Lal finds out what she gets in return.

cards.text: The garage behind Hanna Brook's house in Bristol contains, at a rough count, forty-three bicycles, and only one of them belongs to her. The rest arrive almost every week: left by her gate with notes attached, rescued from skips, or handed over by neighbours who are moving house. Hanna, a former hospital pharmacist, repairs each one and gives it away to a newly arrived refugee family. 'People think the bikes are the point,' she says, wiping oil from her hands onto trousers that were clearly chosen for the purpose. 'They're not, really. The bike is just the excuse.'
cards.question: What does Hanna say about the bicycles she gives away?
choices: They are not the most important part of what she does.
Most of them are donated by local shops.
She keeps the best ones for herself.
They are often too damaged to repair.
cards.highlight: The bike is just the excuse.
cards.why: She says people think the bikes are the point but 'They're not, really. The bike is just the excuse.' The bikes come from gates, skips and neighbours, not shops, so B is wrong.

cards.text: The idea began four years ago, when a Syrian family moved into the flat opposite. Hanna noticed that the father, Karim, walked an hour each way to an English class, and offered him her late husband's old bicycle, which had been hanging on the garage wall for years. The tyres were flat and the chain had rusted solid. Karim spent a whole Saturday helping her fix it, and they had, she says, 'a very long conversation in about forty words of shared language'. By the end of the day the bike worked. A week later, two of Karim's friends knocked on her door.
cards.question: What can we infer from the visit of Karim's friends?
choices: They wanted Hanna to teach them English.
Karim had told them what Hanna had done for him.
They needed help moving into a new flat.
They had come to return the bicycle for Karim.
cards.highlight: A week later, two of Karim's friends knocked on her door.
cards.why: Coming straight after the story of the repaired bike, the friends' visit suggests Karim had told them about it and they hoped for help too. Nothing links them to English lessons, so A is wrong.

cards.text: Hanna knew almost nothing about bicycles at the time. Her husband had always done the repairs, and she had never so much as changed a tyre. So she taught herself, mostly from online videos and a second-hand manual with half the pages missing. Her early repairs, she admits, were not always reliable. One bike lost a pedal on its first trip to the supermarket. Rather than being put off, she found this oddly encouraging. 'It meant I could only get better,' she says. Now she can rebuild a wheel in under an hour and find most problems just by listening.
cards.question: What does 'this' refer to in 'she found this oddly encouraging'?
choices: teaching herself from online videos
her husband doing all the repairs
a bike losing a pedal
rebuilding a wheel in under an hour
cards.highlight: One bike lost a pedal on its first trip to the supermarket.
cards.why: 'This' points back to the sentence just before it: the pedal falling off. Because it was a failure, she calls her reaction 'oddly' encouraging. D is what she can do now, later in the paragraph.

cards.text: Every bike leaves the garage with a lock, a set of lights and a short lesson in the rules of the road, which Hanna gives on the quiet street outside her house. She also insists that each new owner does at least one repair themselves before taking the bike away. Last spring a ten-year-old girl called Amira replaced her own brake cable, then spent the afternoon fixing her younger brothers' bikes without being asked. 'She was much quicker than I was at her age,' Hanna says. 'Much quicker than I am now, to be honest.' Amira still visits on Saturdays, as her unofficial assistant.
cards.question: Why does the writer mention Amira?
choices: to suggest that children should not ride on busy roads
to prove that children learn faster than adults
to explain why Hanna needed to find an assistant
to show how Hanna's rule can give people skills and confidence
cards.highlight: then spent the afternoon fixing her younger brothers' bikes without being asked
cards.why: After the one repair Hanna insists on, Amira went on fixing bikes 'without being asked', so the rule gave her skills and confidence. Hanna's joke about being slower is not the writer's main point, so B is wrong.

cards.text: Not everyone approves. A neighbour once complained to the council about the number of bicycles in the lane, and Hanna had to hide them away for a month. She has also been told, more than once, that she is 'only scratching the surface' of a much bigger problem. She does not disagree. 'Of course a bike doesn't find someone a home or a job,' she says. 'But it gets them to the job interview, and it gets them there on time. And then they ride past my house and ring the bell.' She smiles. 'That's my salary.'
cards.question: What do people mean when they say Hanna is 'only scratching the surface'?
choices: She is making a difficult situation worse.
She is doing very little compared with what is needed.
She is not looking after the bicycles properly.
She is working hard without being paid.
cards.highlight: Of course a bike doesn't find someone a home or a job
cards.why: Hanna agrees that 'a bike doesn't find someone a home or a job', so the phrase means her help is small compared with the whole problem. 'That's my salary' is a joke about the bell, so D is wrong.

cards.text: So what about the one bicycle in the garage that is hers? It is a heavy black machine, about sixty years old, with a basket on the front and a bell that no longer works. It was her husband's, the same one that she once offered to Karim, and he returned it as soon as he could afford a bike of his own. Hanna has repaired it many times but never ridden it further than the end of the road. 'I keep meaning to give it away,' she says, closing the garage door. 'Maybe next year.' She does not sound in any hurry.
cards.question: What does the final paragraph suggest about Hanna?
choices: She plans to start riding the old bike more often.
She wishes she had never lent the bike to Karim.
She is not ready to part with the bike that started it all.
She finds older bicycles harder to repair.
cards.highlight: She does not sound in any hurry.
cards.why: The one bike from the opening is her husband's, the one that started the project. She says 'maybe next year' but 'does not sound in any hurry'. Karim returned it as soon as he could, and nothing suggests regret, so B is wrong.
